notes.read: One big shaggy cow standing in tall grass at sunset, lit from behind and to the right, with a glowing sky, soft violet hills and a green hillside behind. What matters is the cow's mass and its glowing rim; what's hard is the coat, which has to read as hanging locks a beginner can pull, not strands. The lesson should get the background on fast and spend its time on the cow.
notes.order: Back to front: the sky and its clouds, the far hills and the loch, the hillside and the meadow base, then the cow (shape, shading, two passes of locks), its horns and face, the tall grass flicked over its legs, and the brightest lights last. Built without pipeline v4's rule (the gate's other side): every layer runs under what covers it.

stages.name: Blend the sunset sky
steps: Start at the top edge with Sky blue in a thin band across the whole width. The sky covers the whole canvas, from the top edge to the bottom edge.
Pull long side-to-side strokes from edge to edge. Without rinsing, pick up Golden yellow and Pale gold for a broad warm band next, then go back to Sky blue for the rest of the way down.
The warm band sits high, near the top of the canvas, glowing brightest toward the right edge where the low sun is. Sky blue fills the rest down to the bottom edge, with a few soft warm streaks.
Leave no white canvas anywhere: the sky covers it all.
Stop when every join is soft and the canvas reads as blue sky with a glowing band near the top.

stages.name: Dry-brush the orange cloud streaks
steps: Let the sky dry completely first, or the dry brush will drag wet blue into the streaks.
Start in the warm band near the top of the canvas, at the right edge, with Peach orange on a dry brush.
Golden yellow again, but this time on a dry brush in broken streaks instead of a wet blend.
Skim long, flat strokes side to side with light pressure, flat along the bottom and ragged on top. Use Golden yellow for some streaks.
Most of the streaks sit in the right half of the canvas: a cluster of thin ones in the warm band near the top, and a few longer, ragged ones lower down toward the right edge.
Leave most of the blue showing between the streaks, and let the sky show through their broken edges.
Stop when soft warm streaks cross the top band and a few broken ones float lower down, none of them solid.

stages.name: Light the tops of the clouds
steps: Let the streaks from step 2 dry before you start.
Start on the top edges of the cloud streaks in the warm band near the top of the canvas.
The same dry-brush skim as the streaks, now with Pale gold and only along the lit edge of each streak.
Skim Pale gold along the upper edge of each streak with a nearly dry brush, following its long, flat line side to side. Lighten the pressure toward the ends.
The pale paint rides the top of each streak, where the low sun catches it, and softens the ragged edges into the blue. Give the lower streaks the same light touch.
Leave the warm orange showing in the middle and bottom of every streak, and keep the blue between them.
Stop when each streak has a soft, pale upper edge and the streaks look blended into the sky rather than stuck on. It should never become a solid area.

stages.name: Lay in the green hillside
steps: Let the hills and the loch dry first.
Start at the left edge on the ridge, about 3 1/4 in from the top edge, just below the far violet hills.
The same long, level strokes as the loch, now with a big brush and tilted with the slope of the hill.

opening.welcome: You're painting a shaggy highland cow standing in tall golden grass at sunset, with violet hills and a glowing sky behind it. The heart of the painting is the cow's face: its pink nose peeking out from a long, sunlit fringe, framed by two curved horns. Keep the mood warm and quiet, like the last light of a summer evening.
opening.light: The light is a low sun sitting behind the cow, near the horizon. It makes the sky glow gold near the hills, and it catches the edges of the cow's fringe and coat in a bright rim while the face and much of the body stay in soft shadow.

skills.how: Dry brushing means only the tip of a dry brush goes in the paint, skimmed lightly so the marks break up and let the earlier paint show through. It makes the cloud streaks, shades the far hills and puts the final sunlit rim on the cow. If it goes on solid, the brush was too loaded: let it dry and keep each pass lighter.

Curved strokes bend with the shape you're painting, which is what makes a thing look round or sloped. They shape the humps of the far hills, the round body of the cow, its horns and its nose. Let every stroke follow the curve, never straight across it.

Flicking is a quick stroke up from the base of a blade, lifting off as it goes so each mark thins at its tip. It builds the tall grass in passes, darkest first, and pulls it over the cow's legs so the cow stands in the field. Load the brush lightly, or you'll get flat blobs.

opening.road: First you blend the whole sky in one wet go, then dry-brush its warm cloud streaks and light their edges. Next come the far violet hills and a small glowing sliver of loch, kept flat and hazy because they are far away. Then the green hillside, its dabbed bushes and the glowing meadow cover the land, so the cow can be painted straight over them. Most of your time goes on the cow: a flat shape, dark shading, copper and gold locks, then horns and the face. Last, the tall grass is flicked over the cow's legs and the brightest sunlit edges go on once the paint they go over is dry.

the-sky.for: This stage lays the farthest thing first: a soft sunset sky with warm cloud streaks.
the-sky.end: The whole canvas is blue sky with a glowing gold band and soft, pale-edged cloud streaks drifting across it.

the-far-hills.for: This stage sets the far land against the sky: two hazy violet ranges and a sliver of loch.
the-far-hills.end: Two rolling violet ranges cross the sky, the nearer one shaded, with a thin glowing strip of loch at the canvas edge and the streaky sky still filling the rest.

the-hillside-and-meadow.for: This stage builds all the land the cow will stand on: the hillside, its bushes and the meadow.
the-hillside-and-meadow.end: Every bit of canvas past the far hills is now green land: a sloping hillside striped with dark bushes, and a glowing, criss-crossed meadow with no grass blades yet.

the-cows-shape.for: This stage builds the cow as one big shape and gives it its shadows.
the-cows-shape.end: A big, round, dark brown cow stands in the meadow, streaked like shaggy hair, with a lighter face and chest.

the-shaggy-coat.for: This stage gives the cow its long, hanging coat in two passes of locks.
the-shaggy-coat.end: The cow is covered in long copper locks with dark gaps between them and a few small golden glints.

the-horns-and-face.for: This stage adds the horns and the face, the part of the painting the eye goes to first.
the-horns-and-face.end: Two shaded, curved horns rise from the cow's head, and a pink nose with dark nostrils and a mouth peeks out from the fringe.

the-tall-grass.for: This stage flicks the tall grass over the meadow and the cow's legs so the cow stands in the field.
the-tall-grass.end: Dark and olive grass blades rise over the cow's legs and across the meadow, dotted with golden seed heads, bigger in front.

the-last-lights.for: This stage adds the brightest touches of sunlight, last, once the paint they go over is dry.
the-last-lights.end: The finished painting: a bright rim of sunlight glows along the cow's coat, the horns catch a line of light, and a few grass tips shine.

technique_picks.technique_why: A sunset sky, far hills and a grassy field behind one big shaggy cow paint naturally back to front, and every texture here (cloud streaks, dabbed bushes, hanging locks, flicked grass) is one repeated mark a beginner can make.
